I am hesitant to weigh in on discussions about 30+ year old details. I understand enough about memory in general, and mine in particular, to not have great confidence about it. I generally trust Romero’s memory more than mine — I was always a bit jealous of that capability.

In broad terms, multiplayer gaming was right up there with 3D gaming in my grand visions of what I wanted to accomplish. The early FPS games were very much “first person Gauntlet”, and Gauntlet had multiplayer.

I do clearly remember the first time I got two computers running Doom taking to each other. Moving around on one computer and seeing the character move on the other screen was sublime. And then, of course, I shot the other character. Every shared virtual environment inhabited by young men inevitably hosts deathmatch.

I suspect the confusion here may be around the fraction of people that originally bought Doom because of multiplayer. It was almost certainly well under 10%. Maybe under 1%. It wrecked some college networks, but most people didn’t have Ethernet cards or null modem cables. We probably did have some conversations correctly predicting that. Deathmatch was awesome, but most of our players never got to experience it.

Even four games later for Quake 3 Arena, being “deathmatch focused” was a huge internal battle, and not at all obviously viable.

quoted_tweet.author: Aaron Levie
quoted_tweet.text:
It’s almost incomprehensible how wide the distance is between someone who’s working at the frontier with AI and basically everyone else right now. 

The crazy thing is these lines are not converging, but only growing farther apart. If the curve of AI progress had leveled off, it would certainly have given most people and companies time to catch up or implement their workflows in a standardized way. The technology would have neutralized competitive advantage because everyone would be using it the same way.

But what’s happened is the opposite. The curve of AI progress is basically going vertical right now, which means if you had codified your processes 3-6 months ago you’re likely already behind again. Now imagine most companies that kicked into gear a year ago and thought that they were done. Even further behind now.

I’ve never seen a technology in my life and career that improves at this rate, which consequently means you need to upgrade your expectations at a similar rate. Our brains weren’t wired for this, and our organizational change management processes certainly weren’t either.

With any form of recursive self improvement, things just get wilder. It’s a time when you will need to be constantly reevaluating the things that didn’t work just a couple months ago to see if they now can be solved. AI native companies certainly have a strong advantage due to this right now, so now it comes down to can the bigger companies keep up. Wild times.

Your prompt order is a bill.

OpenAI now lets you choose 12-hour prompt caching in the API, so shared instructions, tools and context stay cached at the lower cached-input rate even when requests are hours apart. In Codex and Work, signed-in users get their cache kept with no time limit, and coming back to an old conversation carries no penalty.

A cache only matches an identical prefix. The comparison starts at the first token, and the first difference ends the match.

the default that costs you: a prompt that opens with today's date, the user's name or a timestamp. That one line makes every request look new, so the same long instructions get billed at full price on every call.

the layout that hits the cache:

1. Instructions and rules, word for word identical on every call.
2. Tool definitions and reference documents.
3. Examples.
4. Last: the date, the user, the question.

the check: the API response reports cached_tokens in its usage details. Send the same request twice. If the second one shows zero, something near the top is changing.

I keep long prompts in a fixed template for this reason. Role, rules, format and examples stay put, and only the input slot at the bottom moves.

12-hour retention is built for persistent agents that reuse the same context through a working day.
